title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
description: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, custo
body: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues."What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said."The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs."One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in."You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences."Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.Additional reporting by Henry Moore

title: At least 24 killed after bus collides with truck near Kaziranga National Park
description: The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon. Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous
body: The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon. Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous for its one-horned rhinoceroses.Nagaon is an important agricultural and commercial centre in central Assam, about 120km (74.5 miles) west of Bokakhat by road.Lurinjyoti Gogoi, chief of a regional opposition party, said road safety has long been a major concern in the state."The government must take it up seriously," he said.Road accidents are responsible for thousands of deaths in India every year.In 2023, 172,000 people lost their lives on Indian roads, or 474 a day – roughly one every three minutes.The count increased to 183,382 deaths in 2025.Experts say the crisis is rooted not just in infrastructure but in human behaviour, enforcement gaps and systemic neglect.

title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips,
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China."President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia."The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external."The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media. Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December."Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security."Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

schema.headline: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed

title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
description: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US presiden
body: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.Now the political pressure is building.Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

schema.headline: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House

title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economyByTess
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economyByTessa Wong and Osmond ChiaReporting fromSingaporeA major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.Megaspeed is a case in point.It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.The city-state has had some success in policing this.It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Megaspeed's office in Singapore In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meetingHow Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore."For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said."Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China"."This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

schema.headline: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore

title: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: The general at the centre of Uganda's power struggle
description: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.Ov
body: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency. Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal. Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project"."Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted."The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption. He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive."Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted."The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings."Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job."Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted. He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible. It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly. Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power."The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh,  Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition."The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.For now, Museveni remains in power.But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

schema.headline: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: The general at the centre of Uganda's power struggle

title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
description: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in Ne
body: Figure caption, Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New OrleansByAna FaguySome 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help"."We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.Image source, Getty ImagesThere were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.Image source, Getty ImagesShips have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision."It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

schema.headline: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision

title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery
description: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the wo
body: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again."We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said."We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services."The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem."Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said."In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

schema.headline: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage as it reports broad recovery

title: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb
description: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Za
body: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military  and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations. Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

schema.headline: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb

title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership
description: Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the p
body: Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections. Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomed "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".He added that he was "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he had "the votes to continue as Democratic leader". The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes. The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.Announcing his plans to run in a post on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people"."We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people," he said at a summit in Colorado hosted by majority Democrats. "And we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up." He added: "This country does not belong to the people who can afford to buy influence. It belongs to all of us. And it's time we govern like that."In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party. In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he was an "underdog" but added that he believed the race was "very much in flux".Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.In a post on X, Sanders said he believed Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

schema.headline: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership

title: First catch aborted in SpaceX Starship rocket double-catch test
description: The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.It was suppos
body: The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean.During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely."The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space.The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead, it has splashed down in the ocean.Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it is in space.If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.But it is not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

schema.headline: First catch aborted in SpaceX Starship rocket double-catch test

title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
description: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of
body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow."In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week."Our proposals were almost laughed at."Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire"."The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken."Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.And what of Putin?At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.You can see why.The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatSpanish star Rosalía has ma
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatSpanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux. The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc. The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement awardIt was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution"."It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin GrammysAccepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far"."Long live Argentine folk music," he added.Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.Additional reporting by Abu Bakar YasinListen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys

title: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
description: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secur
body: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory."We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas. "Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026. The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances."Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them. Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa."I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico. She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

schema.headline: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite

title: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
description: Image source, Reuters / Pilar OlivaresImage caption, The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several yearsByJosé Carlos CuetoBBC
body: Image source, Reuters / Pilar OlivaresImage caption, The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several yearsByJosé Carlos CuetoBBC News Mundo in Chiclayo, PeruPope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America. The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff."Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers. "Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago. Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began. "We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique. Image source, Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Pope Leo celebrated Mass in front of a jubilant crowdMany came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional. The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached. They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C. For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight."The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.Image caption, Lisbeth Díaz says Chiclayo is celebrating the Pope's returnPeru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.Image caption, Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horsebackBut for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes."It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela."It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country."So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.Father Miranda also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together."If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".That unity has been on display in the run up to the Mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.Image caption, Father Samuel David Miranda Atoche says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the ChurchNormally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass. Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event. Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff."As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

schema.headline: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
